I've been working this land for 40 years. Four-point-one mu isn't much, but it's mine and I know every corner of it. My husband and one of my sons work in the city now, so mostly it's me managing the fields, sometimes with help from my daughter-in-law during busy periods. I can't afford to take risks — this crop is still part of how we eat and earn.

**My thinking:**

For wheat, I'll plant the full 4.1 mu in October as always. I use improved varieties — the agricultural station has been pushing Jimai 22 and similar for years, and the yields are reliable. Traditional seeds just don't compete anymore. I'll do a base fertilizer application before planting, then topdress at jointing. I always irrigate four times for wheat — the winter freeze irrigation is critical here in Hebei so the roots don't die, then again at green-up, jointing, and heading. Skipping one risks the whole harvest. I'll spray herbicide in spring and fungicide around heading — powdery mildew and scab have been problems in recent years.

For maize, I plant right after wheat harvest in June on the same land. Hybrids are standard now — I've used Zhengdan 958 for years, it performs well. I'll do minimal tillage, just rotary to break up the stubble. Maize gets summer rain so I don't irrigate as much — maybe twice, at seedling establishment if it's dry and definitely at silking. I apply fertilizer in two shots: base and then topdressing at the big bell stage. One herbicide pass early, maybe check for corn borer mid-season.

I'm not going to experiment this year. My knees aren't what they were and I manage mostly alone. Proven inputs, proven varieties, enough irrigation to protect the yield.

For winter wheat I use improved varieties and apply fertilizer in two splits, irrigating four times including the critical freeze irrigation; I spray herbicide and fungicide to protect yield. For summer maize I use hybrid seed and plant immediately after wheat harvest with rotary tillage to clear stubble, relying mainly on summer rain with two supplemental irrigations at seedling and silking stages. I stick to proven varieties and conventional input rates because at my age and with limited labor I cannot afford crop failure or the learning curve of new practices.
